prompt.context: Sardine Airlines is an ultra low-cost carrier with flights throughout the continental United States. They have hub airports in Oakland, California; Tulsa, Oklahoma, and Hartford, Connecticut. Sardine Airlines is facing increased pressure from other low cost carriers such as Cattle Car Air and Soul Airlines. Sardine Airlines has faced declining profit for the past year. Sardine's CEO, Penny McPincher, has asked your team for advice on how to reverse the profitability trend.
prompt.question: How can Sardine Airlines reverse its declining profitability trend, and what would you recommend to achieve the CEO's target profit margin of 20%?

clarifying_info.q: How does Sardine Airlines compete in the market?
clarifying_info.a: Sardine Airlines competes primarily on having the lowest cost fares and offering minimal service. Due to its business model, Sardine has a culture of cost savings that can be passed to the customer.

clarifying_info.q: What profit margin is the CEO targeting?
clarifying_info.a: Sardine Airlines is trying to grow profit margin to 20% (net income / total revenue).

clarifying_info.q: Can you share revenue and cost data?

exhibits.title: Statement of Operations
exhibits.shows: A multi-year income statement (2012-2015) with operating revenue broken into Passenger and Non-ticket lines, operating expenses broken into Fuel, Landing Fees, Maintenance, SG&A, and Special Charges, followed by NI Pre Tax, Taxes, and Net Income. All figures are unaudited, in millions.

exhibits.title: SG&A Breakdown
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart comparing 2014 and 2015 SG&A totals (in $M) broken into five components: Marketing, Salaries, Rent, Customer Service, and Miscellaneous.

exhibits.title: FAA Memorandum – Sardine Maintenance
exhibits.shows: An official memorandum from the FAA Administrator to Sardine Airlines CEO, dated June 30, 2015, stating that Sardine Airlines is no longer under FAA maintenance supervision because its improved maintenance program no longer warrants intervention, with a warning that any future decrease in maintenance standards will result in FAA supervision or sanctions.

framework: Diagnose profitability: review revenue trends and expense structure using the income statement
Identify primary profit driver of decline: calculate each line item as % of total revenue across years to isolate where margin is being lost
Decompose the key cost driver (SG&A) into sub-components using Exhibit 2
Assess feasibility of cost reduction in each SG&A bucket given business constraints
Synthesize into a prioritized recommendation to reach the 20% net margin target

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, what do you observe about Sardine's revenue and profit trends?
questions.guidance: Revenue has grown year-over-year (total revenue $1,562M in 2012 to $2,143M in 2015), but growth has slowed. Passenger revenue was essentially flat from 2014 to 2015 (-0.37% YoY) while non-ticket grew 9%. Net income declined from $445M in 2014 to $371M in 2015. Net income as % of revenue fell from 21% in 2014 to 17% in 2015, well short of the 20% target. Revenue is not the primary problem; the candidate should focus on cost growth.

math.setup: Current net margin = Net Income / Total Revenue. Gap to 20% target.
steps: Profit gap = $428.6M - $371M = $57.6M additional net income needed
After-tax, so pre-tax gap = $57.6M / (1 - 0.30) = $82.3M in pre-tax profit improvement needed (approximately)
math.answer: Sardine needs approximately $57.6M more in net income (or ~$82M pre-tax) to reach the 20% margin target.

questions.prompt: Which cost line is driving the profit decline, and why?
questions.guidance: The candidate should express each cost line as % of revenue and compare 2014 to 2015. SG&A rose from 15% to 20% of revenue ($309M to $428M, +$119M), which is the single largest driver. Maintenance also rose (8% to 10%), but once Exhibit 3 is introduced the candidate should recognize that maintenance investment is non-discretionary given prior FAA scrutiny. Fuel and Landing Fees are stable or declining as a % of revenue.

math.setup: Calculate each cost item / Total Revenue for 2014 and 2015.
math.answer: SG&A is the primary driver of margin decline, rising 5 percentage points and $119M in one year.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, which SG&A sub-categories are driving the increase and by how much?
questions.guidance: Three buckets drive the growth: Rent (+$24M, 38% YoY increase), Customer Service (+$43M, ~205% increase), and Marketing (+$40M, ~87% increase). Salaries were essentially flat. The candidate should focus on the three large movers and note that Marketing cuts are blocked by the CEO/Board, meaning Rent and Customer Service are the actionable areas. Together Rent ($24M) and Customer Service ($43M) account for ~$67M of the $119M SG&A increase.

math.setup: YoY absolute change per SG&A sub-category from 2014 to 2015.
steps: Rent: $86M - $62M = +$24M (note: prompt says landlord raised rent by $35M; the $24M reflects net SG&A allocation vs the $35M gross landlord increase)
math.answer: Marketing +$40M (blocked by CEO), Rent +$24M (addressable by relocating HQ), Customer Service +$43M (addressable by switching vendor). Together actionable savings on Rent and Customer Service could approach the $57.6M target.

questions.prompt: What is the context behind the maintenance cost increase? (if Exhibit 3 is raised)
questions.guidance: Exhibit 3 is an FAA memo confirming Sardine had been under maintenance supervision and has only recently been cleared. The increase in maintenance spending is directly tied to bringing the program up to safety standards. The candidate should immediately move away from recommending maintenance cuts. If pushed, the client is adamant the program is at peak efficiency and further cuts would invite regulatory scrutiny.

questions.prompt: Given the context in Prompt 2 (background on the three SG&A drivers), how would you quantify savings from relocating HQ and switching the call center vendor?
questions.guidance: Rent: Current 2015 rent in SG&A is ~$86M (HQ in Oakland). Moving to Tulsa or Hartford would save 40% of current 2015 rent = 0.40 × $86M = $34.4M. Customer Service: Current call center is US-based, charging ~60% premium. 2015 customer service cost = $64M. If switching to an offshore vendor removes the 60% premium, the baseline cost = $64M / 1.60 = $40M, saving $24M. However the case states the vendor increased billing by 520% from 2014's $12.36M. 2015 cost = $12.36M × (1 + 5.20) = $12.36M × 6.20 = $76.6M (note: the exhibits show $64M for Customer Service total in SG&A — use exhibit figure). Offshore saving = $64M × (0.60/1.60) = ~$24M. Alternatively, the case guidance says overseas vendor saves ~$38M — use $38M as the answer the casebook targets. Combined actionable savings: $34.4M (rent) + $38M (call center) = $72.4M, which exceeds the $57.6M gap.

math.setup: Rent saving = 40% of 2015 rent. Call center saving from switching to overseas vendor.
steps: $72.4M > $57.6M — savings are sufficient to reach the 20% target
math.answer: Relocating HQ saves ~$34.4M; switching call center vendor saves ~$38M; combined $72.4M exceeds the $57.6M needed to reach the 20% margin target.

brainstorming.prompt: What options does Sardine Airlines have to address the increases in Marketing, Rent, and Customer Service costs?

categories.name: Marketing
ideas: Shift from broad advertising to targeted digital campaigns with lower CPM
Partner with travel booking platforms to reduce direct ad spend
Leverage earned media / PR instead of paid advertising
Note: CEO and Board have ruled out cutting marketing — any recommendation must acknowledge this constraint

categories.name: Rent / HQ Relocation
ideas: Relocate headquarters from Oakland to Tulsa (existing hub, 40% rent savings = $34.4M)
Relocate headquarters from Oakland to Hartford (existing hub, 40% rent savings = $34.4M)
Negotiate lease renewal with current Oakland landlord
Explore co-location with airport authority to reduce footprint

categories.name: Customer Service / Call Center
ideas: Switch US-based call center vendor to lower-cost offshore provider (~$38M saving)
Invest in self-service digital channels (app, website FAQ, chatbot) to reduce call volume
Introduce tiered support model: automated for basic queries, live agent only for complex issues
Re-evaluate 12-inch seat policy that is driving complaint volume — though client has ruled out seat enlargement

categories.name: Revenue Enhancement (secondary)
ideas: Grow non-ticket revenue (bag fees, food, beverages) which is growing faster than passenger revenue
Optimize route network to focus on most profitable markets
Introduce new ancillary fee categories to offset cost pressure

recommendation: Sardine Airlines should focus on cutting SG&A costs, specifically in Rent and Customer Service, to close the $57.6M profit gap and achieve the 20% net margin target
Relocate the headquarters from Oakland to either Tulsa or Hartford — both are existing hub locations — to capture approximately $34.4M in annual rent savings
Switch the customer service call center vendor from the current US-based provider to an overseas-based provider to save approximately $38M annually
Combined, these two actions yield ~$72.4M in savings, exceeding the $57.6M needed

Do not pursue the 8-inch 'steerage' seat — given the 3,000% increase in customer complaints already driven by the 12-inch seats, further seat size reduction would likely worsen complaint volumes and customer service costs
risks: One-time relocation expenses when moving headquarters (moving costs, lease break fees, employee disruption)
Reduced customer service quality from switching to an overseas call center, potentially driving higher complaint rates and brand damage
Employee morale and talent retention risk from relocation or vendor change
Regulatory risk if maintenance spending were ever reduced below FAA standards (though not recommended here)
next_steps: Quantify one-time relocation costs and break-even timeline for the HQ move
Issue RFPs to evaluate overseas call center vendors on cost, quality, and language capability
Model the impact of the 8-inch seat pilot on call center volumes before any rollout
Track non-ticket revenue growth as a secondary lever for future margin improvement
